newsitem.title: UK: Mideast VLCC stagnant despite strong Asian demand.
newsitem.headline: Mideast VLCC stagnant despite strong Asian demand.

text.p: Middle East very large crude carriers (VLCC) rates ended the week lower despite strong demand from Japan and Korea and above average fixtures for this time of year, shipping brokers said.
There were some signs of a pick up in VLCC rates for the Mideast/Japan stem by Friday with the 250,000 tonne Erica fetching W50, up from W47.5 for similar tonnage earlier in the week.
Rates for other Far Eastern destinations, however, languished below W50 and brokers blamed an abundance of relets in the region for the weakness.
Brokers Galbraith's said in their weekly tanker report that the total number of fixtures concluded during the week from the region was above 35 deals, higher than average.
"Despite a healthy increase in fixing of large tonnage from the Middle East Gulf, rates showed little or no improvement," brokers E.A. Gibson said in a report.
"This was largely due to a surfeit of Far Eastern relet tonnage which has been created by refinery maintenance in Japan and South Korea," they added.

Galbraith's and Gibson said they believed the Far Eastern market had bottomed out and rates should start to improve. Gibson saw 45 vessels of 13.5 million tonnes available over the next four weeks "which should indicate that rates have at least bottomed out".

Galbraith's said demand was up also for the Middle East/West stem. KPC and Chevron both picked up modern ships, the Regal Unity and Sebu respectively at W45. KPC subsequently took the Arosa, anothern modern double/double but were forced to pay W47.5 on a 275,000 tonner.

Aframax enquiry in the Med was very thin, causing rates to fall to W107 for 80,000 tonne cargoes compared with W120 late last week. One million tonners fared slightly better but also fell back to W90 from W95 by the end of the week.

West African business was also slow with the brief strike by Nigerian port workers at Bonny having an impact. There were only a limited amount of fixtures for Suezmax vessels at around W90 for the U.S. Gulf and W95 for Europe. Galbraith's expected rates to pick up.

"It is generally believed that the West African market will be busier next week and already there are signs that one or two owners are starting to ask for another five points in this area, which they will surely get if recent signs are anything to go by," they said.
Inter-U.K./Cont rates also slipped on low enquiry, with 80,000 tonners dropping to around W90 from W95 last week.
Caribbean rates proved the most reslient with Caribs/upcoast rates for 70,000 tonners holding fast to W220 for much of the week before falling back to W110-W115 by Friday.
